notes.bp: Voice training is an interactional skill, so a useful tool must show a learner what changed while they speak and remain usable in practice.
notes.wh: Resonance is felt and heard, but a display can overwhelm a learner or turn a gradual skill into a misleading single score.
notes.naive: Show raw spectra or prescribe a fixed target value and assume users can interpret it.
notes.ap: Build a browser tool that gives real-time vocal-resonance biofeedback and evaluate whether intended users can complete tasks and understand the feedback.
notes.mech: The study combines real-time acoustic analysis, visual feedback, and a usability evaluation for gender-affirming voice training.
notes.math: The design treats feedback as part of a human learning loop: measurement matters only if a person can notice it, interpret it, and act on it.
notes.ww: The paper reports a working web application and usability findings supporting its use as a training aid.
notes.limits: Small usability sample, task design, browser/audio conditions, and self-report limit claims about long-term learning or clinical outcomes.
notes.title: Web-Based Application for Real-Time Biofeedback of Vocal Resonance in Gender-Affirming Voice Training: Design and Usability Evaluation

notes.bp: A speech system should identify toxic spans in Vietnamese audio without hiding which words triggered the judgment.
notes.wh: Toxicity depends on language, context, and span boundaries; speech recognition errors can change both the words and the location of the alleged harm.
notes.naive: Classify the whole utterance or run a text toxicity model on an imperfect transcript and treat its spans as exact.
notes.ap: Create an audio-based Vietnamese toxic-span task that preserves local evidence and evaluates both detection and boundary selection.
notes.mech: ViToSA builds an audio dataset and task for locating toxic spans in Vietnamese speech utterances.
notes.math: The prediction target is localized: the system must connect acoustic input to a particular interval or word span rather than only assign a sentence label.
notes.ww: The paper reports benchmark results for Vietnamese audio toxic-span detection.
notes.limits: Dataset construction, annotation agreement, language, ASR errors, and social context bound the result; a benchmark score is not a complete safety policy.
notes.title: ViToSA: Audio-Based Toxic Spans Detection on Vietnamese Speech Utterances

notes.bp: Respiratory sounds are noisy measurements of a changing physical process, and a classifier needs to preserve disease-relevant events while suppressing irrelevant noise.
notes.wh: Breath sounds overlap in time and vary by microphone, patient, environment, and pathology; fixed denoising can remove the very irregularity being measured.
notes.naive: Apply one fixed noise filter or classify raw recordings without testing how denoising changes the signal.
notes.ap: Use an adaptive differential denoising procedure whose behavior changes with the observed respiratory signal, then test classification.
notes.mech: The paper proposes adaptive differential denoising for respiratory-sound classification and compares it with less adaptive processing.
notes.math: Denoising is part of the measurement model: the classifier can only learn a clinical distinction if the preprocessing preserves the relevant temporal-acoustic structure.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved respiratory-sound classification with the proposed denoising approach.
notes.limits: Dataset, labels, recording hardware, noise conditions, and evaluation split limit generalization to clinical deployment or diagnosis.
notes.title: Adaptive Differential Denoising for Respiratory Sounds Classification

notes.bp: A spoken-language model trained end to end may learn new tasks while forgetting how to perform tasks it already knew.
notes.wh: Speech, text, vocabulary, and task behavior are updated together; reducing forgetting can also reduce learning of the new objective or distort the shared representation.
notes.naive: Train only on the new data, freeze everything, or assume a larger model automatically retains old abilities.
notes.ap: Compare mitigation strategies for catastrophic forgetting during end-to-end spoken-language-model training, including how data and parameter updates are controlled.
notes.mech: The study evaluates forgetting-mitigation strategies for end-to-end training of spoken language models.
notes.math: The core tradeoff is retention versus adaptation: an update is useful only if it improves the new task without erasing previously learned speech-language behavior.
notes.ww: The paper reports comparative forgetting and adaptation results across the tested strategies.
notes.limits: Tasks, training order, model size, data mixture, and retention metrics bound the conclusions; results do not establish lifelong learning in open deployment.
notes.title: Analyzing Mitigation Strategies for Catastrophic Forgetting in End-to-End Training of Spoken Language Models

notes.bp: A speaker-recognition backend must decide whether recordings belong to the same person, while evaluation rankings can change with scoring, calibration, and trial composition.
notes.wh: A benchmark result is not only an embedding result: backend assumptions determine how scores are normalized and how errors are traded off.
notes.naive: Compare systems using one unexamined score or treat the best embedding as automatically the best verification system.
notes.ap: Analyze the ABC classification backends used for NIST SRE24 and separate representation quality from backend scoring behavior.
notes.mech: The paper studies backend choices for speaker classification/verification in the NIST SRE24 setting.
notes.math: Verification is a decision pipeline: embeddings, score computation, calibration, and operating point jointly produce the accepted/rejected decision.
notes.ww: The paper reports how the analyzed backends behave on the NIST SRE24 evaluation conditions.
notes.limits: Benchmark protocol, language/channel conditions, calibration, and chosen operating points limit claims beyond SRE24.
notes.title: Analysis of the ABC Classification Backends for NIST SRE24

notes.bp: A speech codec should use few bits while preserving speech quality and should let a downstream system change speaker identity without accidentally carrying the original identity through the code.
notes.wh: Compression and identity are entangled: a code that preserves every detail spends bits, while a code that removes identity may damage linguistic content or naturalness.
notes.naive: Compress a standard speaker-dependent representation and assume the decoder will separate identity later.
notes.ap: Learn a low-bitrate discrete code that is decoupled from speaker identity, then condition decoding on the desired speaker.
notes.mech: LSCodec targets low-bitrate, speaker-decoupled discrete speech coding for controllable reconstruction or conversion.
notes.math: The code is a bottleneck with a division of labor: linguistic/acoustic content crosses the bottleneck, while speaker identity is supplied separately at decoding.
notes.ww: The paper reports low-bitrate codec and speaker-decoupling results on its reconstruction/conversion evaluations.
notes.limits: Bitrate, speaker set, decoder, datasets, and disentanglement tests bound the claim; identity leakage can remain outside the tested conditions.
notes.title: LSCodec: Low-Bitrate and Speaker-Decoupled Discrete Speech Codec

notes.bp: Contextual biasing should help a recognizer spell a user's rare keyword, but it should not turn every acoustically similar word into that keyword.
notes.wh: Synthetic training examples can be plentiful yet unrealistic; a fixed cost for all keywords ignores how often each keyword is confused and how context changes the error.
notes.naive: Add a uniform decoding bonus or generate random keyword examples without modeling which confusions matter.
notes.ap: Use a keyword-aware cost function when training synthetic contextual-biasing data so difficult and useful examples receive the right pressure.
notes.mech: The paper improves synthetic-data training for contextual biasing with a keyword-aware cost function.
notes.math: The training objective changes the data's influence according to the keyword-level error structure; the goal is targeted correction rather than blanket bias.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved contextual-biasing performance for the proposed synthetic-data objective.
notes.limits: Keyword lists, synthetic-data quality, language, decoder, and evaluation distribution limit generalization; better keyword recall can still create false activations.
notes.title: Improving Synthetic Data Training for Contextual Biasing Models with a Keyword-Aware Cost Function

notes.bp: Parkinson's speech can show changes in both how sounds are produced and how language is organized, so one signal family may give an incomplete picture.
notes.wh: Acoustic and linguistic symptoms vary across speakers and tasks, and changes can be correlated without one causing the other.
notes.naive: Use only a speech-rate/acoustic score or only a transcript-based linguistic score as a complete disease marker.
notes.ap: Measure acoustic and linguistic production synchronously in the same speech material and examine their joint relationship.
notes.mech: The study synchronizes analysis of abnormal acoustic and linguistic production in Parkinson's speech.
notes.math: Synchronous observation aligns two levels of behavior in time, allowing co-occurrence to be studied without pretending that either level alone explains the condition.
notes.ww: The paper reports coordinated acoustic and linguistic findings in Parkinson's speech.
notes.limits: Cohort, task, disease stage, annotation, and statistical design limit clinical generalization; association is not diagnosis or causation.
notes.title: Synchronous analysis of abnormal acoustic and linguistic production in Parkinson's speech
